BENEFIT CORPORATION — FORMATION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

BENEFIT CORPORATION PURPOSE AND ELECTION DECLARATION
The name of the corporation is Acme, Inc. This corporation is a benefit corporation. Acme, Inc. is formed in accordance with the General Corporation Law, and, in addition, elects to be subject to Part 13 (commencing with Section 14600) of Division 3 of Title 1 of the California Corporations Code. Acme, Inc. shall have the purpose of creating general public benefit, meaning a material positive impact on society and the environment, taken as a whole, as assessed against a third-party standard, from the business and operations of Acme, Inc. This purpose is in addition to, and may be a limitation on, Acme, Inc.'s purpose of engaging in any lawful act or activity for which a corporation may be organized under the General Corporation Law. promoting access to affordable clean energy The initial street address of Acme, Inc. is 123 Main St, San Francisco, CA 94103. The name of Acme, Inc.'s initial agent for service of process in California is Jordan Lee. The agent's street address in California is 123 Main St, San Francisco, CA 94103.

WHAT A BENEFIT CORPORATION IS AND THE GENERAL PUBLIC BENEFIT PURPOSE REQUIREMENT
California's Corporations Code contains a distinct statutory part governing the for-profit "benefit corporation" — Part 13 of Division 3 of Title 1, Corp. Code §§ 14600-14631 — that is a different corporate form both from an ordinary for-profit corporation formed only under the General Corporation Law and from the differently-named nonprofit "public benefit corporation," which is formed under a separate part of the Nonprofit Corporation Law, has no shareholders, and may not distribute profits. By statutory definition, a "benefit corporation" is "a corporation organized under the General Corporation Law that has elected to become subject to this part and whose status as a benefit corporation has not been terminated as provided in this part" — meaning the entity starts as an ordinary for-profit corporation and becomes a benefit corporation only by an affirmative election, not automatically. Once elected, the statute requires the corporation to "have the purpose of creating general public benefit," a term the same statute defines as "a material positive impact on society and the environment, taken as a whole, as assessed against a third-party standard, from the business and operations of a benefit corporation." This general-public-benefit purpose is layered onto, not a substitute for, the corporation's ordinary for-profit purpose: the statute states that it is "in addition to, and may be a limitation on," the corporation's purpose under the General Corporation Law's own purpose provision, and a benefit corporation may, but need not, also adopt one or more narrower "specific public benefit" purposes alongside the required general one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Benefit corporation” means a corporation organized under the General Corporation Law that has elected to become subject to this part and whose status as a benefit corporation has not been terminated as provided in this part."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(a), (c), California benefit corporation statute, definitions of "benefit corporation" and "general public benefit" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14601.)
  "A benefit corporation shall have the purpose of creating general public benefit. This purpose is in addition to, and may be a limitation on, the corporation’s purpose under Section 206 and any specific purpose set forth in its articles in accordance with subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14610(a), California benefit corporation statute, the required general public benefit purpose (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14610.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state defines and structures this specific for-profit corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation, and not a claim that every state with a benefit corporation statute defines or structures the form identically; benefit corporation statutes vary by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 14601 and Cal. Corp. Code § 14610, and are treated as two independent sources; within the first citation, the two quoted subsections, (a) and (c), are both drawn from the same section, § 14601, and are not independent of each other. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself elect benefit corporation status for any corporation, and does not determine federal tax treatment of any corporation, which is a separate question this document does not address.

REQUIRED CONTENT OF BENEFIT CORPORATION ARTICLES OF INCORPORATION
A California benefit corporation's formation filing is not a separate document from an ordinary for-profit corporation's articles — it is formed "in accordance with Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 200) of Division 1," the same General Corporation Law formation chapter every for-profit corporation uses — but the benefit corporation statute adds specific required content on top of that ordinary chapter: "the articles shall also state that the corporation is a benefit corporation and shall identify any specific public benefit" the corporation has adopted. A separate section of the same statutory part supplies the exact required language: "the articles of incorporation of a benefit corporation shall contain the following statement: 'This corporation is a benefit corporation.'" That same section also permits, but does not require, the articles to identify one or more specific public benefits as the corporation's purpose, and states that doing so does not narrow the corporation's separate obligation to also pursue general public benefit. Both of these requirements are additional to, not substitutes for, the content requirements that already apply to every for-profit corporation's articles under the General Corporation Law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A benefit corporation shall be formed in accordance with Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 200) of Division 1 except that the articles shall also state that the corporation is a benefit corporation and shall identify any specific public benefit adopted pursuant to Section 14610."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14602, California benefit corporation statute, formation under the General Corporation Law plus the added statement and specific-benefit identification requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14602.)
  "In addition to the provisions required by Section 202, the articles of incorporation of a benefit corporation shall contain the following statement: “This corporation is a benefit corporation.”"
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14610(b), California benefit corporation statute, the required articles statement electing benefit corporation status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14610.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state's required formation-document content for this specific type of for-profit corporation looks like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation, and required content for a benefit corporation's articles varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 14602 and Cal. Corp. Code § 14610(b), and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself file anything with the California Secretary of State, and does not itself elect benefit corporation status for any corporation.

ANNUAL BENEFIT REPORT: CONTENT, DELIVERY TO SHAREHOLDERS, AND PUBLIC POSTING
California's benefit corporation statute requires an annual benefit report, and states what it must contain, who must receive it, and when. On content, the statute states that "a benefit corporation shall deliver to each shareholder an annual benefit report" that must include, among other required elements, "an assessment of the overall social and environmental performance of the benefit corporation, prepared in accordance with a third-party standard applied consistently with any application of that standard in prior benefit reports or accompanied by an explanation of the reasons for any inconsistent application" — and the statute is explicit that "the assessment does not need to be audited or certified by a third party." A separate section of the same statutory part requires the report to include a further, specific statement: the board of directors must prepare, "for inclusion in the annual benefit report to shareholders required by Section 14630, a statement indicating whether, in the opinion of the board of directors, the benefit corporation failed to pursue its general, and any specific, public benefit purpose in all material respects during the period covered by the report." On timing and recipients, the report "shall be sent annually to each shareholder within 120 days following the end of the fiscal year of the benefit corporation or at the same time that the benefit corporation delivers any other annual report to its shareholders" — so delivery runs to shareholders, not to the general public, by default. Public availability is nonetheless required in a different way: "a benefit corporation shall post all of its benefit reports on the public portion of its Internet Web site, if any," though compensation and certain financial or proprietary information may be omitted from that publicly posted version.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An assessment of the overall social and environmental performance of the benefit corporation, prepared in accordance with a third-party standard applied consistently with any application of that standard in prior benefit reports or accompanied by an explanation of the reasons for any inconsistent application. The assessment does not need to be audited or certified by a third party."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14630(a), California benefit corporation statute, duty to deliver an annual benefit report to shareholders and the required third-party-standard assessment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14630.)
  "The benefit report shall be sent annually to each shareholder within 120 days following the end of the fiscal year of the benefit corporation or at the same time that the benefit corporation delivers any other annual report to its shareholders."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14630(b), California benefit corporation statute, 120-day annual delivery deadline to shareholders (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14630.)
  "A benefit corporation shall post all of its benefit reports on the public portion of its Internet Web site, if any, except that the compensation paid to directors and any financial or proprietary information included in the benefit report may be omitted from the benefit report as posted on the Internet Web site."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14630(c), California benefit corporation statute, requirement to post benefit reports on the corporation's public website (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14630.)
  "The board of directors of a benefit corporation shall prepare for inclusion in the annual benefit report to shareholders required by Section 14630, a statement indicating whether, in the opinion of the board of directors, the benefit corporation failed to pursue its general, and any specific, public benefit purpose in all material respects during the period covered by the report."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14621(a), California benefit corporation statute, required board statement on whether the public benefit purpose was pursued (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14621.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own annual-report content, delivery, and public-posting requirements for this specific type of for-profit corporation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and annual benefit reporting requirements, if any, vary by state. The first three citations below are all drawn from subsections of the same section, Cal. Corp. Code § 14630(a), (b), and (c), and are treated as one source, not three independent ones; the fourth citation, Cal. Corp. Code § 14621(a), is an independently enacted section and is treated as a second, independent source. This document is informational only: it does not itself prepare, deliver, or post any benefit report on behalf of any corporation.

DIRECTOR DUTIES: REQUIRED CONSIDERATION OF NON-SHAREHOLDER INTERESTS
California's benefit corporation statute states a director's duty of care in language close to the General Corporation Law's ordinary standard — acting "in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the benefit corporation and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances" — but then adds a list of interests a director must consider that reaches well beyond shareholder profit. The statute requires that in discharging their duties and considering the corporation's best interests, "the board of directors, committees of the board, and individual directors of a benefit corporation shall consider the impacts of any action or proposed action upon all of the following": the shareholders; "the employees and workforce of the benefit corporation and its subsidiaries and suppliers"; customers, "as beneficiaries of the general or specific public benefit purposes of the benefit corporation"; "community and societal considerations, including those of any community in which offices or facilities of the benefit corporation or its subsidiaries or suppliers are located"; and "the local and global environment." This is a mandatory consideration requirement, not merely a permitted one — the statute elsewhere makes certain other factors optional for a director to consider, but places shareholders, employees, customers, community, and the environment in the mandatory list.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A director shall perform the duties of a director including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the benefit corporation and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14620(a), (b), California benefit corporation statute, director duty of care and required consideration of non-shareholder interests (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14620.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state's benefit corporation law modifies the ordinary director duty of care for this specific corporate form — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's directors, and how (or whether) a state modifies director duties for a benefit-type corporation varies by state. The single citation below combines two subsections of the same section, Cal. Corp. Code § 14620(a) and (b), and is treated as one source; the statute contains further subsections addressing director liability limits and reliance on others' reports that are not quoted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself impose or interpret any specific director's duties and does not evaluate whether any specific director's conduct complied with this statute.

BENEFIT ENFORCEMENT PROCEEDINGS: EXCLUSIVE REMEDY, STANDING, AND AVAILABLE RELIEF
California's benefit corporation statute channels claims about a benefit corporation's public-benefit obligations into a single, narrowly defined procedural vehicle rather than leaving them to ordinary shareholder litigation. The statute defines a "benefit enforcement proceeding" as "a claim or action relating to any of the following: (1) Failure to pursue the general public benefit purpose of the benefit corporation or any specific public benefit purpose set forth in its articles. (2) Violation of a duty or standard of conduct imposed on a director pursuant to this part. (3) Failure of the benefit corporation to deliver or post an annual benefit report as required by Section 14630." A separate section makes that vehicle exclusive and limits who may use it: "no person may bring an action or assert a claim against a benefit corporation or its directors or officers under this chapter except in a benefit enforcement proceeding," and such a proceeding "may be commenced or maintained only" directly by the benefit corporation itself, or derivatively by a shareholder, a director, a person or group owning 5 percent or more of an entity of which the benefit corporation is a subsidiary, or other persons specified in the corporation's own articles or bylaws — a narrower list than the general universe of persons who might otherwise sue a corporation. On remedy, the same section provides that "if the court in a benefit enforcement proceeding finds that a failure to comply with this part was without justification, the court may award an amount sufficient to reimburse the plaintiff for the reasonable expenses incurred by the plaintiff, including attorney's fees and expenses, in connection with the benefit enforcement proceeding" — an expense-reimbursement remedy tied to the litigation itself, not a monetary damages award against the corporation for failing to create public benefit, which the same statutory part separately forecloses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Benefit enforcement proceeding” means a claim or action relating to any of the following: (1) Failure to pursue the general public benefit purpose of the benefit corporation or any specific public benefit purpose set forth in its articles. (2) Violation of a duty or standard of conduct imposed on a director pursuant to this part. (3)  Failure of the benefit corporation to deliver or post an annual benefit report as required by Section 14630."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(b), California benefit corporation statute, definition of "benefit enforcement proceeding" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14601.)
  "No person may bring an action or assert a claim against a benefit corporation or its directors or officers under this chapter except in a benefit enforcement proceeding."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14623(a), (b), (d), California benefit corporation statute, exclusivity of the benefit enforcement proceeding, standing to bring one, and the expense-reimbursement remedy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14623.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one state defines, channels, and remedies claims about a benefit corporation's public-benefit obligations — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's litigation, and enforcement mechanisms for a benefit-type corporation, including who has standing and what remedy is available, vary by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(b) and Cal. Corp. Code § 14623; within the second citation, the quoted subsections (a), (b), and (d) are all drawn from the same section, § 14623, and are not independent of each other. This document is informational only: it does not itself bring, defend, or evaluate the merits of any claim, and it does not determine whether any specific person has standing to bring a benefit enforcement proceeding.

TERMINATING BENEFIT CORPORATION STATUS: MINIMUM STATUS VOTE AND DISSENTING SHAREHOLDER RIGHTS
California's benefit corporation statute sets a heightened, defined vote threshold for a corporation to drop out of benefit corporation status, rather than leaving that decision to whatever vote an ordinary articles amendment would otherwise require. The statute provides that "a benefit corporation may terminate its status as a benefit corporation and cease to be subject to this part by amending the corporation's articles to delete the provision required by Section 14602" — the statement electing benefit corporation status — but "the amendment shall not be effective unless the amendment is adopted by at least the minimum status vote," and further provides that a shareholder who dissents from that amendment may require the corporation to purchase the shareholder's shares at fair market value, following the same statutory dissenters'-rights procedure used for a reorganization. "Minimum status vote" is itself a defined statutory term, and for a corporation it requires more than an ordinary majority: "in addition to any other approval or vote required by Division 1 (commencing with Section 100) or the articles of incorporation," every class or series of shareholders is entitled to vote "regardless of any limitation stated in the articles or bylaws on the voting rights of any class or series," and "the corporate action shall be approved by the outstanding shares of each class or series by at least two-thirds of the votes, or greater vote if required in the articles of incorporation, that all shareholders of the class or series are entitled to cast on that action." The same defined "minimum status vote" threshold also governs a corporation electing into benefit corporation status in the first place, and certain reorganizations, conversions, and asset-sale transactions that would have the effect of terminating that status.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A benefit corporation may terminate its status as a benefit corporation and cease to be subject to this part by amending the corporation’s articles to delete the provision required by Section 14602. The amendment shall not be effective unless the amendment is adopted by at least the minimum status vote."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14604(a), California benefit corporation statute, terminating benefit corporation status by articles amendment and resulting dissenters' rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14604.)
  "The shareholders of every class or series shall be entitled to vote on the corporate action regardless of any limitation stated in the articles or bylaws on the voting rights of any class or series. (B) The corporate action shall be approved by the outstanding shares of each class or series by at least two-thirds of the votes, or greater vote if required in the articles of incorporation, that all shareholders of the class or series are entitled to cast on that action."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(d)(1)(A)-(B), California benefit corporation statute, definition of "minimum status vote" for a corporation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=14601.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's own vote threshold and dissenters'-rights procedure for exiting this specific corporate status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's amendment process, and whether a state imposes a heightened vote threshold for terminating benefit corporation status, and what that threshold is, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 14604(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 14601(d)(1)(A)-(B), and are treated as two independent sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself amend any corporation's articles, does not itself terminate benefit corporation status for any corporation, and does not calculate the specific vote threshold or fair market value applicable to any specific corporation's shares.

The statute defines a "benefit enforcement proceeding" as "a claim or action relating to any of the following: (1) Failure to pursue the general public benefit purpose of the benefit corporation or any specific public benefit purpose set forth in its articles. (2) Violation of a duty or standard of conduct imposed on a director pursuant to this part. (3) Failure of the benefit corporation to deliver or post an annual benefit report as required by Section 14630." A separate section makes that vehicle exclusive and limits who may use it: "no person may bring an action or assert a claim against a benefit corporation or its directors or officers under this chapter except in a benefit enforcement proceeding," and such a proceeding "may be commenced or maintained only" directly by the benefit corporation itself, or derivatively by a shareholder, a director, a person or group owning 5 percent or more of an entity of which the benefit corporation is a subsidiary, or other persons specified in the corporation's own articles or bylaws — a narrower list than the general universe of persons who might otherwise sue a corporation. On remedy, the same section provides that "if the court in a benefit enforcement proceeding finds that a failure to comply with this part was without justification, the court may award an amount sufficient to reimburse the plaintiff for the reasonable expenses incurred by the plaintiff, including attorney's fees and expenses, in connection with the benefit enforcement proceeding" — an expense-reimbursement remedy tied to the litigation itself, not a monetary damages award against the corporation for failing to create public benefit, which the same statutory part separately forecloses.

expectedJSON.body: California's benefit corporation statute sets a heightened, defined vote threshold for a corporation to drop out of benefit corporation status, rather than leaving that decision to whatever vote an ordinary articles amendment would otherwise require. The statute provides that "a benefit corporation may terminate its status as a benefit corporation and cease to be subject to this part by amending the corporation's articles to delete the provision required by Section 14602" — the statement electing benefit corporation status — but "the amendment shall not be effective unless the amendment is adopted by at least the minimum status vote," and further provides that a shareholder who dissents from that amendment may require the corporation to purchase the shareholder's shares at fair market value, following the same statutory dissenters'-rights procedure used for a reorganization. "Minimum status vote" is itself a defined statutory term, and for a corporation it requires more than an ordinary majority: "in addition to any other approval or vote required by Division 1 (commencing with Section 100) or the articles of incorporation," every class or series of shareholders is entitled to vote "regardless of any limitation stated in the articles or bylaws on the voting rights of any class or series," and "the corporate action shall be approved by the outstanding shares of each class or series by at least two-thirds of the votes, or greater vote if required in the articles of incorporation, that all shareholders of the class or series are entitled to cast on that action." The same defined "minimum status vote" threshold also governs a corporation electing into benefit corporation status in the first place, and certain reorganizations, conversions, and asset-sale transactions that would have the effect of terminating that status.
